nameStory: The species name 'mundusnovus' literally means 'new world' in Latin, reflecting its classification as a New World shrimp species. The common name 'glass shrimp' comes from their remarkably transparent bodies that seem almost invisible in water, like living pieces of clear glass.
description: Glass shrimps are tiny, nearly transparent crustaceans that look like miniature versions of the shrimp you might eat at dinner. They have long antennae, ten legs (including claws), and bodies that are so clear you can often see their internal organs through their skin. Most glass shrimps grow to about half an inch to an inch long, making them quite small compared to their marine cousins.

idTips.label: Transparent body
idTips.description: The body is remarkably clear and glassy, often appearing almost invisible in water except for faint outlines and visible internal structures

idTips.label: Long antennae
idTips.description: Two pairs of very long, thread-like antennae that are often longer than the body itself and constantly moving to sense the environment

idTips.label: Small claws
idTips.description: Tiny pincers on the front legs that are delicate and used for picking up small food particles

idTips.label: Swimming motion
idTips.description: Moves with quick, darting motions using rapid tail flicks, often staying near vegetation or structure rather than open water

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Very small, typically less than an inch long, about the size of your thumbnail or smaller

habitat: Found in shallow coastal waters, tidal pools, and brackish areas where fresh and salt water mix along New England's coast. They prefer areas with plenty of vegetation like eelgrass beds or rocky areas with algae growth that provide both food and shelter from predators.

seasonality.spring: More active as waters warm, often found in shallow tidal areas and beginning to reproduce.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity season when they're easiest to spot in warm, shallow waters during low tide exploration.
seasonality.fall: Still active but may move to slightly deeper or more protected waters as temperatures begin to drop.
seasonality.winter: Much less active and harder to find, likely in deeper waters or protected crevices.

funFact: Despite being nearly invisible, glass shrimps can actually change their transparency levels slightly - becoming more opaque when stressed or threatened, almost like a natural cloaking device that can be turned up or down!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other small glass shrimp species in tide pools, but the exact identification often requires close examination of antenna length and body proportions. Remember: if it's tiny, transparent, and has long antennae in a tide pool, you're looking at some type of glass shrimp.
contextualKnowledge: This species is extremely rare in New England with only one recorded observation, so any sighting would be quite significant. It's possible this represents either a range extension or a very localized population that's easily overlooked due to the shrimp's transparent nature.
compareHints: Compared to the more common Marsh Grass Shrimp and Eastern Grass Shrimp in New England waters, Palaemon mundusnovus is distinguished by subtle differences in antenna proportions and body shape. However, given its rarity, any glass shrimp found is more likely to be one of the common species unless examined by an expert.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Rockpool prawns can be distinguished from other Palaemon glass shrimp in New England by their habitat preference for rocky tide pools rather than salt marshes or estuaries.
Oriental Shrimp can be distinguished from other Palaemon species by their exceptionally long antennae and more pronounced rostrum.

Among its glass shrimp relatives, the marsh grass shrimp is the only one with those distinctive orange eyestalks — the Eastern grass shrimp lacks this coloration, while the Daggerblade grass shrimp has different body proportions.
Eastern Grass Shrimp are distinguished from their close relatives like Daggerblade Grass Shrimp by their freshwater habitat preference, while Daggerblade species prefer brackish or saltwater marshes.

Among its glass shrimp relatives, the daggerblade stands out with its distinctive brownish spots scattered across the transparent body - other Palaemon species in New England waters tend to be more uniformly colored or have different spot patterns.
